# AMALGAMATION Weeks 8–10: Step-by-Step SOP for Qualitative Data Analysis

**Course:** BMGT-8044 / RSCH-V8927 Doctoral Project Development — Framework Development  
**Study:** Generic qualitative inquiry of U.S. SME IT and network managers’ IT disaster-recovery governance on external platforms (ITDRPaaS)  
**Instrument:** `ITDR-GQI-INT-v0.1.1` ([gqi-semistructured-interview-guide.md](gqi-semistructured-interview-guide.md))  
**Analytic method:** Hybrid deductive–inductive codebook thematic analysis (Fereday & Muir-Cochrane, 2006)  
**CAQDAS (support only):** Delve (Delve, Ho, & Limpaecher, n.d.)  
**Sample (locked):** **n = 12** participants  
**Companions:** [chapter-iii-methodology.md](chapter-iii-methodology.md) · [collection-analysis-revision-packet.md](collection-analysis-revision-packet.md) · [symbols-definitions-refs.md](symbols-definitions-refs.md)

**How this file was filled.** The Weeks 8–10 amalgamation template supplied a five-phase analysis SOP, a Chapter III construction blueprint, and placeholder Chapter III drafts. Those placeholders have been replaced with this study’s locked procedures. Bracketed generic Insert-placeholders, NVivo/MAXQDA as the method, reflexive thematic analysis as the method, sampling by Mitchell types, a 12-to-20 sample range, and lived-experience-as-method language are not used.

**Do not write:** “Data will be analyzed using Delve.” Name the method first, then name Delve as storage and audit support.

## Detailed summary (what this SOP locks)

This SOP is the paste-ready operations manual for Chapter III sections 3.1–3.11. It converts the amalgamation template into study-specific steps that a second reader can audit.

1. **Design.** Generic qualitative inquiry (Caelli et al., 2003; Kahlke, 2014; Percy et al., 2015) using critical-incident interviews (Flanagan, 1954; Chell, 2004; Butterfield et al., 2005). The object of study is a manager’s account of one named ITDRPaaS recovery or test event, not the essence of a lived experience.
2. **Questions.** Implied **PQ1** (stakeholder-claim management and salience shifts) and **PQ2** (enactment as decision rights, escalation, and recoverability proof). Official RQ wording replaces those labels when locked; the unit of analysis does not change.
3. **Framework role.** Mitchell et al. (1997) power, legitimacy, and urgency are sensitizing probes. They are not sampling screens, not spoken question stems, and not Chapter IV theme titles. Leverage is the enacted combination of those attributes in the named incident. It is not a fourth salience attribute.
4. **Sample (locked).** Criterion-based purposive sampling of 12 U.S. SME IT, network, systems, infrastructure, or operations managers (Percy et al., 2015). Firm size is 10–200 personnel. Inclusion requires one qualifying event in 36 months on an external recovery platform. Vendors-only and executives with no operational recovery role are excluded. Adequacy is justified by information power (Malterud et al., 2016), not by statistical power and not by a claim that the twelfth interview saturates the gap (Naeem et al., 2024).
5. **Collection.** One 60–75 minute recorded video interview per participant, instrument `ITDR-GQI-INT-v0.1.1`, plus optional artifact Paths A/B/C.
6. **Analysis.** Hybrid codebook thematic analysis (Fereday & Muir-Cochrane, 2006) with STRUCTURAL, FRAMEWORK_DEDUCTIVE, and BOUNDARY codes imported first; EMERGENT stays empty until meaning units are locked (Aronson, 1994; Taylor & Bogdan, 1998). Themes are patterned-meaning claims named in Chapter IV.
7. **Trustworthiness.** Credibility, dependability, confirmability, and transferability (Lincoln & Guba, 1985; Korstjens & Moser, 2018; Nowell et al., 2017). Member checking is factual only and time-bounded at seven calendar days.
8. **Ethics.** Capella IRB before recruitment; individual outreach; identifier stripping; encrypted RAW storage separate from the CLEAN/ANALYTIC path.

## Five-phase analysis SOP (filled)

Qualitative analysis follows a progressive distillation from raw incident talk to patterned-meaning claims. The phases below replace the template’s generic Saldaña/NVivo wording with this study’s locked method.

| Phase | Core objective | Key activities and tools | Methodological output |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| Phase 1: Familiarization and preparation | Establish immersion in each CLEAN transcript and artifact map | Produce a verbatim transcript; strip identifiers; member-check facts; read end-to-end without naming themes; write the 24-hour reflexive memo | CLEAN transcript; artifact-map row; reflexive memo |
| Phase 2: First-cycle coding | File excerpts and apply the imported template | Import the nested start-list from `docs/notion/templates/codebook.csv` into Delve; apply STRUCTURAL and FRAMEWORK_DEDUCTIVE codes where a concrete example or documented boundary exists | Codebook v1.0 applied; snippet URLs |
| Phase 3: Meaning-unit lock and second-cycle categorization | Move from codes to practice-claim sentences, then to categories | Lock meaning units before any EMERGENT code or theme name (Aronson, 1994; Taylor & Bogdan, 1998); add inductive child codes only after that lock; group units only when they describe the same salience-to-assurance bargain | Meaning-unit table; categories (still unnamed as themes) |
| Phase 4: Thematic synthesis | Abstract categories into claims that answer PQ1 and PQ2 separately | Name themes as patterned-meaning sentences, not topic headings; map each theme to PQ1 or PQ2; do not write that themes “emerged” (Braun & Clarke, 2021; Lester et al., 2020) | Thematic matrix for Chapter IV |
| Phase 5: Validation and stopping audit | Verify grounding and document why recruitment ended at 12 | Negative and boundary cases per construct; codebook versioning; dated CSV nest; record whether the twelfth interview still changed the meaning-unit inventory (Naeem et al., 2024; Carcary, 2020) | Audit trail; stopping rationale for n = 12 |

## 3.1 Introduction and chapter overview

Chapter II established the theoretical and empirical background for stakeholder-claim management in IT disaster recovery on external platforms and located the gap: U.S. SME IT and network managers must handle competing restoration claims without a clear account of how authority and proof are enacted under time pressure. Chapter III specifies the operational methods that will collect and analyze managers’ accounts of one named recovery or test event so that Chapter IV can report patterned-meaning findings and Chapter V can interpret them.

The purpose of this generic qualitative inquiry is to describe how those managers account for stakeholder-claim management and salience shifts in one named ITDRPaaS recovery or test event, and how those shifts are enacted as decision rights, escalation, and defensible proof (Caelli et al., 2003; Kahlke, 2014; Percy et al., 2015; Mitchell et al., 1997). This chapter therefore outlines:

1. The philosophical stance and justification for generic qualitative inquiry with a critical-incident interview stance.
2. The role of the researcher, positionality, and reflexive memoing.
3. Criterion-based purposive sampling with a locked sample of 12 participants, justified by information power.
4. The unpublished interview instrument `ITDR-GQI-INT-v0.1.1` and the artifact pipeline.
5. Hybrid codebook thematic analysis, meaning-unit lock, and the Delve audit nest.
6. Trustworthiness operations (Lincoln & Guba, 1985).
7. Ethical protections, Capella IRB submission, and data-handling rules.

Official research-question wording has not been locked. Until it is, the two implied project questions are labeled PQ1 and PQ2. Replace those labels with the approved wording without changing the unit of analysis.

**Implied project questions**

- **PQ1.** How do U.S. SME IT and network managers describe stakeholder-claim management and salience shifts (power, legitimacy, urgency) during ITDRPaaS recovery or testing incidents?
- **PQ2.** How do those shifts get enacted as decision rights, escalation pathways, and evidentiary / recoverability-assurance standards that managers can defend to stakeholders?

**Unit of analysis.** One U.S. SME IT, network, systems, infrastructure, or operations manager recounting one qualifying disruption, failover, recovery test, or operational recovery in the preceding 36 months in which an external recovery platform or managed recovery service was used.

Chapter III plans that chain. It does not claim final themes. Theme titles, patterned-meaning claims, and answers to PQ1 and PQ2 belong in Chapter IV. Interpretation, implications, and limitations belong in Chapter V.

## 3.2 Research design and methodological justification

### 3.2.1 Philosophical worldview

The study is situated in an interpretivist / constructivist stance: meaning is produced in managers’ accounts of organizational events, decisions, and artifacts, not measured as a variable (Creswell & Poth, 2018; Percy et al., 2015). That stance does not convert the study into phenomenology. The chapter therefore does not use “lived experience,” “essence,” “epoché as the method,” or “voices” as analytic claims.

### 3.2.2 Generic qualitative design rationale

Generic qualitative inquiry is the congruent design because the object of study is managers’ patterned descriptions of external events, decisions, artifacts, and conditions (Caelli et al., 2003; Kahlke, 2014; Percy et al., 2015; Capella University, n.d.-c). GQI permits theoretically informed interview items when those items stay in manager language and when the constructs that informed them are not treated as conclusions (Percy et al., 2015). That permission is why Sets L and A–F can be built from stakeholder-salience and enactment constructs without converting the study into a confirmatory test of Mitchell et al. (1997).

The design is not an audit. NIST, ISO, and BCM materials may appear as industry context, and a manager may name them during an incident account. They are not coding systems. Artifacts are not scored for compliance (Creswell & Poth, 2018).

### 3.2.3 Critical-incident interview stance

The interview stance is the critical incident technique, not a saturation-driven interview method (Flanagan, 1954; Chell, 2004; Butterfield et al., 2005). CIT is used because the gap is operational: how competing stakeholder claims were handled when restoration had to be ranked, delayed, or declared done. A named event supplies a bounded story in which salience can shift and in which decision rights, escalation, and proof can be observed as enacted, including when they were not used.

Guest et al. (2006) is not the interview method. That source is reserved for the later stopping discussion only.

### 3.2.4 Framework role: sensitizing, not confirmatory

Stakeholder identification and salience theory specifies that managers’ attention to claims is a function of power, legitimacy, and urgency (Mitchell et al., 1997). Subsequent work tested and refined that mechanism and is used as build-on literature, not as a replacement for the original definitions (Agle et al., 1999; Neville et al., 2011; Parent & Deephouse, 2007). Recoverability assurance is treated as decision-relevant, reviewable evidence that prioritized services can be restored within tolerance (Lowry et al., 2025; Park et al., 2023; bibliographic details pending verification).

Those sources sit on the Constructs and What We Know nodes. They do not pre-write Chapter IV themes. In analysis they justify a deductive start-list. Inductive codes are added only after meaning units are locked (Aronson, 1994; Fereday & Muir-Cochrane, 2006; Taylor & Bogdan, 1998).

Leverage (`Lev`) is the enacted combination of power, legitimacy, and/or urgency in the named incident. It is not a fourth Mitchell attribute. Mitchell type names (`dormant`, `discretionary`, `demanding`, `dominant`, `dangerous`, `dependent`, `definitive`) stay in the researcher-only leverage memo. They are not Delve theme titles and they are not sampling quotas.

## 3.3 Role of the researcher, positionality, and reflexivity

### 3.3.1 The researcher as the primary instrument

In this single-researcher dissertation, the researcher is the primary instrument of collection, coding, and synthesis (Creswell & Poth, 2018; Pezalla et al., 2012). The researcher conducts the 60–75 minute interviews, produces CLEAN transcripts, applies the imported codebook in Delve, locks meaning units, and writes Chapter IV claims. Delve does not perform the analysis.

That role has two risks that this SOP treats as Gap-data threats: (a) supplying a salience word the participant has not used, and (b) treating a written plan or a vendor name as “real proof” faster than the incident account warrants. The mitigations are a written protocol, skip-if-covered rules, a coverage checklist, a 24-hour reflexive memo, empty EMERGENT until meaning-unit lock, and required boundary cases.

### 3.3.2 Positionality

The researcher is a Capella doctoral candidate studying SME IT disaster-recovery governance. Domain fluency (IT operations, recovery platforms, incident talk) is an insider resource for hearing manager language. The researcher does not recruit through a supervisor, an employer’s command chain, or a vendor account manager, and does not hold decision authority over any participant. That outsider constraint is both an ethical protection and a data-quality protection: supervisor-visible invitation would raise the risk that contested authority and failed-proof talk—the exact material PQ2 requires—would be withheld or sanitized.

This SOP does not invent years of service, a named employer, or a completed expert-panel biography. Those details, if used, belong in the researcher’s IRB protocol and personal statement, not as fabricated methods facts.

### 3.3.3 Reflexive memo (write within 24 hours)

Bracketing in this GQI is procedural, not a phenomenological epoché (Moustakas is not the method). After each interview the researcher answers five lines:

1. Where did I almost supply a salience word the participant had not used?
2. Which claim did I privately prefer (owner, auditor, platform, manager)?
3. Which artifact did I treat as “real proof” too quickly?
4. What boundary case did this session add or still lack?
5. What question did I skip that the coverage checklist still needs?

## 3.4 Participant selection, sampling strategy, and information power

### 3.4.1 Target population

The population is U.S. IT, network, systems, infrastructure, or operations managers in small and medium enterprises who have a direct role in disaster-recovery coordination that uses an external recovery platform, managed recovery service, ITDRPaaS, or a functionally equivalent cloud-recovery capability. Firm size is bounded at 10 to 200 personnel so that the study stays inside SME governance rather than large-enterprise command structures. The population is not vendor staff whose only role is to operate the platform for clients, and it is not executives with no operational recovery role.

Inclusion requires at least one disruption, failover, recovery test, or operational recovery in the preceding 36 months in which that external platform or managed service was used. That incident is the interview’s unit of talk. A manager who cannot name a qualifying event is not in the sample.

### 3.4.2 Sampling strategy: criterion-based purposive sampling

This study uses a nonprobability, criterion-based purposive sampling strategy to select information-rich participants whose roles and recent recovery experience align with the research purpose (Percy et al., 2015; Creswell & Poth, 2018). Criterion-based purposive sampling is appropriate because the aim is a focused account of that phenomenon, not a statistically representative sample.

Stakeholder-salience attributes are **not** used as inclusion screens and are **not** used to quota latent, expectant, and definitive stakeholder classes. Those typologies remain researcher-only memo values after the interview (Mitchell et al., 1997). Using them as sampling quotas would pre-write the sample as a confirmatory test of the theory.

### 3.4.3 Inclusion and exclusion criteria

| Screening category | Operational inclusion | Methodological justification |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Geography and firm size | U.S. enterprise of 10–200 personnel | Keeps the case inside SME governance |
| Role | Active IT, network, systems, infrastructure, or operations management role | Direct operational recovery responsibility |
| Platform experience | Direct responsibility for, or participation in, IT disaster-recovery coordination that uses an external platform or managed recovery service | Matches the gap (platform-mediated recovery) |
| Recency | At least one disruption, failover, recovery test, or operational recovery in the preceding 36 months | Supplies a named CIT event |
| Language and format | Willing to complete a 60–75 minute English video interview and a seven-day factual transcript check | Collection depth and dependability |
| Exclusion | Vendor-only employed; no platform-mediated recovery experience; no named event in 36 months; supervisor, employer command chain, or vendor account manager as the recruitment path | Protects operational focus and PQ2 data quality |

### 3.4.4 Sample size determination — n = 12 locked

Qualitative sample size is not determined by statistical power calculations (Vasileiou et al., 2018). **The sample for this study is locked at 12 participants.** Twelve is the planned recruitment target specified for the detailed screening and interview process. It is a starting plan, not a finding that the gap is closed, and it is not a claim that saturation occurs at the twelfth interview.

Sample adequacy is justified by information power (Malterud et al., 2016). Information power is expected to be relatively high on all five dimensions:

| Information-power dimension | This study’s evaluation | Implication for n = 12 |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Study aim | Narrow: enactment of stakeholder-claim management in one class of SME ITDRPaaS event | A focused aim supports a small, information-rich sample |
| Sample specificity | Dense: U.S. SME IT/network (or equivalent) managers with a named 36-month platform event | Specific participants increase information per interview |
| Theoretical framework | Established sensitizing lens (Mitchell et al., 1997) plus PQ2 enactment probes | Theory-informed dialogue without a closed questionnaire |
| Dialogue quality | Strong: 60–75 minute CIT protocol with skip-if-covered probes | High qualitative density per case |
| Analysis strategy | In-depth hybrid codebook TA and cross-case meaning-unit reduction | Intensive analysis favors a manageable corpus |

Guest et al. (2006) may be cited only in the stopping discussion, as evidence that some interview studies have observed early code stability in relatively homogeneous samples. It is not used to justify the CIT protocol, the sample size in advance, or a claim that 12 interviews suffice.

Stopping is an analytic decision guide applied to the locked corpus of 12 (Naeem et al., 2024). After each interview the researcher records whether new meaning units, categories, or thematic variations relevant to PQ1 and PQ2 still appeared, and whether at least one boundary case per construct exists across the corpus. If the twelfth interview is still changing the meaning-unit inventory, that fact is documented in the audit trail and treated as a limitation in Chapter V. The locked n is not expanded in this plan. The final participant count (12, or fewer if recruitment fails inclusion) and the rationale for ending recruitment are written into the study audit trail (Carcary, 2020).

### 3.4.5 Recruitment and access protocols

Candidates are approached individually through professional networks, practitioner associations, and professional social platforms. The researcher does not recruit through a supervisor, an employer’s command chain, or a vendor account manager. Organizational gatekeeper rosters and supervisor-visible invitation lists are not used.

| Phase | Action | Operational procedure |
| --- | --- | --- |
| 1 | Institutional approval | Submit the protocol to the Capella University IRB. No outreach before written approval. |
| 2 | Individual identification | Approach candidates through professional networks, associations, and professional social platforms. |
| 3 | Eligibility screen | Confirm role, firm-size band, platform role, and a named event in 36 months. Exclude vendor-only staff. |
| 4 | Consent and scheduling | Email the informed-consent form. After signed electronic consent, schedule a 60–75 minute English video interview. Assign `P##` before the call. |
| 5 | Inclusion fail | If the candidate cannot name a qualifying incident, thank and close. Do not continue from a generic “how we usually recover” account. |

Optional confidential peer nomination is permitted only if it does not travel through a supervisor or vendor account manager.

## 3.5 Instrumentation, protocol review, and field calibration

### 3.5.1 Primary instrument

The primary instrument is the unpublished GQI semi-structured interview guide *Where leverage sits*, instrument ID `ITDR-GQI-INT-v0.1.1` (Walker, 2026). It does not create a new theoretical reference and does not displace Mitchell et al. (1997) or CIT sources. Spoken questions use manager language: pull, pressure, right to ask, time-critical, who made the call, what counted as proof. Theoretical labels stay in the researcher codebook and in the leverage memo (Percy et al., 2015; Capella University, n.d.-d).

The session is timed at 60–75 minutes:

| Segment | Items | Function |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Minutes 0–3 | Ethics script | Consent to record; optional artifacts; factual member check |
| Minutes 3–18 | Q0 (required) | Critical-incident opening; one named event |
| Minutes 18–55 | Set L, then Sets A–F | Locate leverage, then power, legitimacy, urgency, decision rights, escalation, proof |
| Minutes 55–70 | Q-close and artifact request | Who had to be convinced, and with what |

**Q0.** Please walk me through one specific disruption, failover, recovery test, or operational recovery in the last 36 months where an external recovery platform or managed recovery service was used. Power, legitimacy, urgency, leverage, and proof are not introduced in Q0.

**Set L.** Who actually moved restore order or could have stopped it (L1), what supplied that pull (L2), and what the manager would have done differently without it (L3).

**Sets A–C.** Power, legitimacy, and urgency examples only if Set L or Q0 did not already supply a concrete example.

**Sets D–F.** Decision rights, escalation, and evidentiary / recoverability proof (PQ2).

**Q-close.** Whether anything about who had to be convinced, and with what, remains unasked.

Skip-if-covered is a procedure, not a convenience. After a skip, the coverage checklist is marked “covered in Q0” or “covered in L.” A set is not skipped because the topic feels familiar. It is skipped only when a concrete example already exists in the record.

Boundary cases are valid data. Nothing escalated, restoration accepted with no reviewable proof, a low-power claim that still won, and pull that the manager cannot locate are coded as `no_escalation`, `no_reviewable_proof`, `low_power_claim_won`, and `pull_unlocated`. They are not failed interviews.

Allowed probes only: *What would be an example of that?* *Please say more about that moment.* *Who else was in that conversation?* *What did you do next?* Silence after a thin answer. Forced choices are not offered (“power or legitimacy,” “NIST or BCM,” yes/no theory labels).

### 3.5.2 Alignment of implied questions to protocol items

| Question | Protocol items | Construct role |
| --- | --- | --- |
| PQ1 | Q0, L1–L3, A1–A3, B1–B2, C1–C2 | Claim attention and salience shifts; leverage location |
| PQ2 | D1–D2, E1–E2, F1–F3, Q-close | Decision rights, escalation, evidentiary standards, recoverability assurance |
| Both | Artifact Paths A/B/C; coverage checklist | Formal intent versus enacted proof |

The seven labels (power, legitimacy, urgency, decision rights, escalation, evidentiary standards, recoverability assurance) plus leverage are sensitizing constructs. They are not predetermined theme titles.

### 3.5.3 Secondary instrument: artifacts as context

Eligible objects include an internal disaster-recovery plan, escalation matrix, recovery-test record, ticket, integrity check, or authorization action. External frameworks such as NIST or BCM are recorded only when the manager names them, and only as context.

| Path | When | Capture | Do not |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| A. Redacted share | Participant can send a screenshot, PDF excerpt, or ticket print | File as `P##_ART##`; strip identifiers on receipt | Score against NIST/ISO/BCM |
| B. Verbal reconstruction | Participant cannot share the file | Type, who used it, who ignored it, whether it counted as proof | Invent contents the participant did not state |
| C. No artifact | Participant names none | Record “no reviewable artifact named” as a recoverability-assurance boundary | Treat as missing data that invalidates the interview |

Path A has a 14-calendar-day window. If nothing arrives, the row is recoded as Path B from session notes. Refusing to share a document does not end the interview.

### 3.5.4 Protocol review and field calibration

This protocol was refined through the BMGT-8044 Data Analysis Practice 2 rehearsal and the Alignment Map revision packet. A separate three-person faculty “expert panel” and a completed two-person pilot are **not** claimed as finished facts in this SOP.

If the supervisory committee or IRB requires a formal pilot, one or two individuals who meet inclusion criteria will be interviewed and excluded from the locked n = 12 corpus. The pilot would test timing (60–75 minutes), comprehension of manager-language stems, recorder backup, and whether Q0 stays on one named event. Pilot transcripts would not be imported into the Chapter IV meaning-unit table.

---

## 3.6 Data collection procedures and field administration

Each of the 12 interviews is one-to-one video, in English, audio- and video-recorded, with a running-notes backup. If the recorder fails, the session is stopped and rescheduled. The interview is not continued from memory.

| Phase | Timeline | Actions |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Pre-session | Before the call | Confirm signed consent; confirm inclusion; assign `P##`; open blank coverage checklist, leverage-memo row, and artifact-map row; test recorder |
| Rapport and ethics | Minutes 0–3 | Read the ethics script. If permission to record is refused, stop and destroy any partial file. |
| CIT opening | Minutes 3–18 | Q0. If the participant stays with “how we usually recover,” ask them to remain with one event. If several events are named, ask for the most vivid or the one in which the recovery decision was hardest. |
| Topical sets | Minutes 18–55 | Set L, then A–F only if a concrete example is still missing. Mark skip-if-covered. |
| Close | Minutes 55–70 | Q-close; artifact request; remind of the seven-day factual check. |
| Post-session | Within 24 hours | Export recording to encrypted RAW storage; complete reflexive memo; start transcription path. |

A session is complete for Alignment Tracking only when each construct row on the coverage checklist has a concrete example or a documented skip-plus-boundary. Completeness is a collection standard. It is not a finding.

If the participant becomes distressed, the researcher pauses, offers to skip or stop, and does not press for graphic incident detail.

## 3.7 Qualitative data analysis plan and coding taxonomy

### 3.7.1 Declaration of method

The analytic method is **hybrid deductive–inductive codebook thematic analysis** (Fereday & Muir-Cochrane, 2006). That method is required because this study’s Alignment Map spine needs (a) a map from implied PQ1 and PQ2 onto instrument items, (b) a versioned codebook that another reader can inspect, and (c) an auditable chain from excerpt to code to category to theme. Fereday and Muir-Cochrane integrated a theory-informed template of codes with data-driven inductive codes. This study uses the same hybrid logic: FRAMEWORK_DEDUCTIVE and BOUNDARY codes are the template; EMERGENT child codes are added only after meaning units are locked.

This is a **single-researcher dissertation**. Default trustworthiness tactics are an audit trail, codebook versioning, negative and boundary cases, reflexive memos, and referential adequacy (Lincoln & Guba, 1985; Nowell et al., 2017). Cohen’s kappa and other intercoder reliability statistics are not part of the default design. If the committee later requires a second coder, ICR is reported as a codebook-communication check only (O’Connor & Joffe, 2020). ICR will not be mixed with a claim that the study is doing Braun and Clarke’s reflexive thematic analysis.

Braun and Clarke (2019, 2021, 2022) are cited for quality of thematic practice, not as the analytic method:

- Codes are not themes.
- Themes are patterned meanings, not topic headings such as “Governance” or “Power.”
- The write-up does not say that themes “emerged.”
- Frequency of a code is not evidence of importance.

Practice 2 from the BMGT-8044 sequence still governs theme naming: lock meaning units that state a practice claim before any theme name is written (Aronson, 1994; Taylor & Bogdan, 1998; Walker, 2026).

### 3.7.2 Why this method and not the adjacent alternatives

| Adjacent choice | Why it is not the method |
| --- | --- |
| Reflexive thematic analysis (Braun & Clarke, 2019, 2021, 2022) | Reflexive TA does not use a start-list codebook as the spine, and it is incompatible with ICR as a quality claim. This study needs RQ mapping and a versioned codebook. |
| Purely inductive TA with no template | Would hide the theoretically informed instrument and would not give an auditable PQ1/PQ2 map. |
| Purely deductive coding that “confirms” Mitchell et al. (1997) | Would pre-write findings and would violate Practice 2. |
| Content analysis / NIST–ISO–BCM scoring | Would convert GQI accounts into an audit. |
| “Analyzed using Delve” or “analyzed using NVivo” | Names the store as if it were the method. |

### 3.7.3 Data preparation, transcription, and CAQDAS management

Preparation follows a three-state path. Delve is the store for the CLEAN and ANALYTIC states. It is not the analytic method.

**RAW.** The recording, running notes, and any artifact files as received. RAW files contain identifiers. They are stored in an encrypted, password-protected directory that is not copied into the public repository or into the Notion CSV nest.

**CLEAN.** A verbatim transcript is produced from the recording. The researcher audits the transcript against the audio (Poland, 2002). Person names, employer names, vendor names, and product names are replaced with `P##`, role only, `SME-A`, and `Platform-1`. Speaker labels are inserted so Delve can split speakers. The CLEAN transcript is the file imported to Delve. Descriptors set at import are `participant_id`, `role_band`, `incident_type`, `firm_size_band`, and `instrument_version`. Descriptors are filters. They are not findings.

**ANALYTIC.** Codes, memos, and snippet URLs are applied inside Delve on the CLEAN transcript. The leverage diagnostic, skip reasons, boundary flags, and reflexive notes are memos linked to snippets. Interval exports of Codes and Snippets are dropped into `docs/notion/interval-backups/YYYY-MM-DD/` with an append-only `update-log.csv` row (Carcary, 2020).

Member checking occurs on the CLEAN transcript, not on ANALYTIC theme names. The de-identified transcript is sent within ten days. The participant has seven calendar days to mark factual corrections of sequence, roles, and artifact type. Participants may not delete a de-identified contested recovery decision from the analytic file. Non-response after seven days is recorded as “no factual corrections returned,” and analysis proceeds.

### 3.7.4 Analytic steps (adapted hybrid codebook TA)

The steps adapt Fereday and Muir-Cochrane (2006) to a single-researcher GQI with a CIT corpus of 12 interviews. Dual-coder “code reliability” is not Stage 2 of the default design.

1. **Develop the code manual.** Import the nested start-list in [notion/templates/codebook.csv](notion/templates/codebook.csv). Each FRAMEWORK_DEDUCTIVE and BOUNDARY code already states what it means, what it is not, an example type, and that it is not a theme title.
2. **Apply STRUCTURAL and FRAMEWORK_DEDUCTIVE codes to CLEAN transcripts.** Tag excerpts by PQ1/PQ2, context, and unanticipated content, then apply sensitizing probes where a concrete example or a documented boundary exists. Co-occurrence is not used to name themes.
3. **Lock meaning units before any EMERGENT code or theme name.** A meaning unit is a practice-claim sentence grounded in a named excerpt (Aronson, 1994; Taylor & Bogdan, 1998). Until that sentence exists, the EMERGENT parent stays empty.
4. **Add inductive (EMERGENT) codes** for patterned claims that the template does not already name. Do not copy `power`, `legitimacy`, `urgency`, or `leverage_location` into EMERGENT.
5. **Group related meaning units into categories** only when they describe the same salience-to-assurance bargain, not merely the same recovery topic.
6. **Name themes as claims.** A theme is a patterned-meaning sentence that can be evidenced with excerpts and limited by at least one negative or boundary case across the 12-interview corpus (Braun & Clarke, 2021; Nowell et al., 2017).
7. **Synthesize two separate answers.** One answer addresses PQ1 (claim attention and salience shifts). The other addresses PQ2 (enactment as decision rights, escalation, and proof). A single “governance” theme is not an answer to either question.
8. **Export and backup.** Codes, snippets, and memos are exported to the dated CSV nest. Code renames, merges, and drops are memoed the same day.

### 3.7.5 Delve nested start-list (import; do not treat as themes)

```
STRUCTURAL
  PQ1_claim_attention
  PQ2_enactment
  CONTEXT
  UNANTICIPATED
FRAMEWORK_DEDUCTIVE  (sensitizing; not findings)
  leverage_location
  power
  legitimacy
  urgency
  decision_rights
  escalation
  evidentiary_standards
  recoverability_assurance
BOUNDARY
  no_escalation
  no_reviewable_proof
  low_power_claim_won
  pull_unlocated
EMERGENT
  (empty until meaning units locked)
```

### 3.7.6 Meaning-unit table

| MU | Meaning-claim (practice sentence, not a noun) | Inclusion bound | Confirming excerpt (`P##` + role band + incident type — no firm name) | Artifact row (if any) | Negative / boundary case | Later theme (filled in Step 6 only) |
| --- | --- | --- | --- | --- | --- | --- |
| MU1 |  |  |  |  |  | — |

Required: at least one boundary case per sensitizing construct across the 12-interview corpus (for example, a manager who never escalated; a restoration accepted with no reviewable proof; a low-power stakeholder whose claim still won).

Relatedness test for every proposed grouping: *Do these units describe the same bargain?* Same bargain example: executive pressure reordered restore priority **and** the written RTO was ignored **and** “up” was declared without an integrity check. Same topic, not same bargain: “we used the cloud failover tool” and “we had a DR plan.”

### 3.7.7 Ten control rules

1. **Method first, software second.** Name hybrid codebook thematic analysis, then name Delve as CAQDAS storage and audit support.
2. **Codes are not themes.**
3. **Themes are claims.**
4. **Do not write that themes “emerged.”**
5. **Frequency is not importance.**
6. **Lock meaning units before theme names.**
7. **Leverage is not a fourth salience attribute.**
8. **Mitchell type names stay in memos.**
9. **NIST, ISO, and BCM are context.**
10. **Chapter III plans; Chapter IV reports; Chapter V interprets.** Guest et al. (2006) is not the interview method. The locked n is 12.

### 3.7.8 Operational determination of stopping (not automatic saturation at 12)

Data collection is planned for 12 interviews. Saturation is not treated as a trustworthiness badge that 12 interviews automatically earn (Malterud et al., 2016; Naeem et al., 2024). After each interview the researcher updates a stopping table:

| Interview (`P##`) | New meaning units on the salience-to-assurance bargain? | New BOUNDARY flags? | Codebook change the same day? | Notes |
| --- | --- | --- | --- | --- |
| P01 | Y/N | Y/N | Y/N |  |
| … |  |  |  |  |
| P12 | Y/N | Y/N | Y/N | Rationale for ending recruitment |

Code saturation (no novel first-cycle codes) and meaning saturation (no new dimensions on existing categories) may be described in the audit trail (Guest et al., 2006, stopping discussion only). Neither threshold is pre-declared as reached at interview 12.

---

## 3.8 Trustworthiness and methodological rigor

This project uses the qualitative criteria of credibility, dependability, confirmability, and transferability (Lincoln & Guba, 1985; Korstjens & Moser, 2018; Nowell et al., 2017). Reporting will be checked against SRQR items and, where they fit a single-researcher interview study, against COREQ items that do not require multiple coders as a quality condition (O’Brien et al., 2014; Tong et al., 2007). Checklists are reporting aids. They are not the analytic method.

| Trustworthiness dimension | Quantitative counterpart (do not use as the method term) | Operational procedures in this study | Audit artifact |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| Credibility | Internal validity | One named CIT event; coverage checklist; factual seven-day member check; boundary cases retained | Coverage checklist; `P##_MC` file; BOUNDARY codes |
| Transferability | External validity | Rich description of role band, firm-size band (10–200), platform type, and incident type without naming organizations. No claim that 12 U.S. SME managers represent all ITDRPaaS settings. | Contextual profile; inclusion table |
| Dependability | Reliability | Written protocol; versioned codebook; Delve snippet URLs; dated CSV nest (Carcary, 2020) | `update-log.csv`; codebook versions |
| Confirmability | Objectivity | 24-hour reflexive memo; evidential anchoring of every Chapter IV theme in excerpts; empty EMERGENT until meaning-unit lock | Reflexive memos; quote-to-theme crosswalk |

Member checking is limited to factual accuracy so that contested recovery decisions are not edited out of the CLEAN file. Participants do not receive theme titles for approval.

Peer debriefing with the dissertation chair, if scheduled, audits codebook logic and theme-as-claim wording. It does not replace the audit trail.

---

## 3.9 Ethical assurances, IRB compliance, and human-subjects protection

### 3.9.1 IRB

The study will be submitted to the Capella University Institutional Review Board before recruitment. Data collection begins only after written approval. Protocol ID is recorded as pending until issued. Amendments to the instrument, recruitment script, or consent form are submitted before use.

The study is designed as minimal risk: the interview concerns professional recovery decisions. Organizational disclosure risk is treated as a Gap-data threat, not only as a compliance item.

### 3.9.2 Informed consent and voluntary participation

Participation is voluntary. After eligibility is confirmed, the informed-consent form is emailed. Signed electronic consent is required before the interview is scheduled. The opening script reconfirms permission to record. Participants may skip any question or stop at any time without penalty.

### 3.9.3 Anonymity, confidentiality, and storage

| Object | Rule |
| --- | --- |
| Participant ID | `P##` assigned before the call |
| People | Role only (`CFO`, `owner`, `help-desk lead`) |
| Employer / client / city | `SME-A`, `site-1` |
| Vendor / product / platform | `Platform-1`, `Vendor-1` |
| Ticket / account identifiers | `TICKET-##` |
| RAW files | Encrypted, password-protected directory; researcher-only; not in the public repository |
| CLEAN / ANALYTIC | Delve plus dated CSV nest; no RAW identifiers |
| Master key | Stored separately from CLEAN files |
| Retention | Follow Capella IRB conditions; destroy identifiers when the policy allows |

File set per participant: consent PDF, recording, verbatim transcript, de-identified transcript, Artifact Map, Path A files (if any), member-check file, reflexive memo.

### 3.9.4 Threat-to-Gap-data matrix

| Ethical / quality threat | How it deletes Gap data | Mitigation |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Sharing DR plans, tickets, or vendor names | Manager withholds proof and escalation talk (PQ2) | Artifact Path B or C is a full interview; refusal never ends the session |
| Dual identifiability (person + firm + vendor) | Decision-rights talk is sanitized | `P##` codes; strip firm/vendor/product/city; encrypted directory |
| Supervisor-visible recruitment | Official plan is performed as “the truth” | Individual outreach; no participation list visible to a boss |
| Member checking as political edit | Contested proof is deleted | Seven-day factual-correction window only |
| Researcher loyalty to seven codes | Findings replay Mitchell et al. | Sensitizing list + meaning-unit table + post-interview reflexive memo |
| Recording failure | Lost incident narrative | No memory-only session; reschedule |
| Manager self-justification treated as proof | Assurance becomes rhetoric | Code “what I told stakeholders” separately from “what artifact existed” |

### 3.9.5 Belmont alignment

| Belmont principle | Risk in this GQI | Operational safeguard |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Respect for persons | Organizational pressure to participate | Capella IRB; written consent; recorded permission to record; right to skip or stop |
| Beneficence | Workplace exposure of contested recovery decisions | Identifier stripping; optional artifacts; factual-only member check |
| Justice | Burden falling on vendor staff or on one employer | Criterion-based inclusion of operational SME managers; vendor-only excluded; no supervisor list |

No monetary inducement is specified in this SOP. If the IRB later approves a nominal token, it will be documented as a protocol amendment.

## 3.10 Chapter III versus Chapter IV versus Chapter V

| Object | Chapter III | Chapter IV | Chapter V |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| PQ1 / PQ2 (or official RQs) | Stated as questions to be answered | Answered with evidenced themes | Interpreted against the gap and literature |
| FRAMEWORK_DEDUCTIVE codes | Imported as sensitizing probes | Cited only as the start-list that collected examples | Not restated as if they were findings |
| Meaning units | Procedure for locking them | Displayed as evidenced claims | Not re-analyzed as new data |
| Categories / themes | Planned, unnamed | Named as patterned meanings; limited by boundary cases | Discussed, not newly named |
| n = 12 | Locked recruitment target; information-power justification | Corpus size reported; stopping table summarized | Limitation if the twelfth interview still changed the inventory |
| Delve / CSV nest | Named as audit infrastructure | Used to locate excerpts | Not a contribution |

---

## 3.11 Chapter summary

Chapter III specifies a generic qualitative inquiry that uses critical-incident interviews with U.S. SME IT and network managers who can name one ITDRPaaS recovery or test event in 36 months. **The sample is locked at 12 participants** and is justified by information power rather than by automatic saturation. The instrument `ITDR-GQI-INT-v0.1.1` locates leverage in that event and then follows the same incident into decision rights, escalation, and recoverability proof, using skip-if-covered rules and boundary cases.

The analytic method is hybrid deductive–inductive codebook thematic analysis (Fereday & Muir-Cochrane, 2006), adapted for a single researcher. Delve is the CAQDAS that stores CLEAN transcripts, the versioned codebook, memos, and snippet URLs. It does not analyze the data. STRUCTURAL, FRAMEWORK_DEDUCTIVE, and BOUNDARY codes are imported as filing and sensitizing devices. EMERGENT stays empty until meaning units are locked. Theme names, patterned-meaning claims, and answers to PQ1 and PQ2 are reserved for Chapter IV. Interpretation is reserved for Chapter V.

---

## Paste-ready sampling block (n = 12 locked)

This study will use a nonprobability, criterion-based purposive sampling strategy to select information-rich participants whose roles and recent recovery experience align with the research purpose (Percy et al., 2015). The target population is U.S. IT, network, systems, infrastructure, or operations managers in small and medium-sized enterprises of 10 to 200 personnel who have direct responsibility for, or participation in, IT disaster recovery that uses an external recovery platform, managed recovery service, ITDRPaaS, or a functionally equivalent cloud-recovery capability. Inclusion requires at least one disruption, failover, recovery test, or operational recovery in the preceding 36 months in which that external capability was used. Individuals employed only by a vendor, or who lack direct platform-mediated recovery responsibility, are excluded. Criterion-based purposive sampling is appropriate because the aim is a focused account of that phenomenon, not a statistically representative sample.

The sample is locked at 12 participants. Sample adequacy will not be determined by statistical power. It will be justified by information power: a narrow aim, a highly specific participant population, theoretically informed but not closed-ended dialogue, and an in-depth thematic analysis strategy (Malterud et al., 2016). Twelve is the planned recruitment target, not a finding that the gap is closed.

Recruitment and preliminary analysis will proceed through the locked sample of 12. Stopping is documented as an analytic decision: the researcher records whether additional interviews within that corpus still contribute new meaning units, categories, or thematic variation relevant to the research questions (Naeem et al., 2024). Guest et al. (2006) may be cited only as background that some homogeneous interview studies have observed early code stability; they are not used to claim that 12 interviews suffice in advance. The final participant count and the rationale for ending recruitment will be recorded in the study audit trail (Carcary, 2020).
